title: Connecting your coding agent
summary: First access, registration, separate frontend implementations and project-local MCP connections on Windows, macOS and Linux.
markdown:
# Connecting your coding agent

## 1. Reach the portal and register

A new Windows recruit gets the **first-access ZIP** from the backend team's DEV Control Center before using the portal.
Extract all files and double-click `START-HERE.cmd`. Compare its CA SHA-256 with the fingerprint supplied separately
by the backend team. It checks TCP, the server's pinned certificate and `/docs/`, trusts the CA for your Windows user,
and opens registration. It contains no account password or MCP key. No administrator shell is needed.
If it fails, send its diagnostic report to the backend/network team. A script cannot fix access-point isolation, VLANs,
a wrong server IP or a stopped gateway. It does not change your network profile, disable firewalls or add static ARP.
`DestinationHostUnreachable` alone does not prove which layer failed. Changing a client profile is not a general fix
for reaching an outbound HTTPS server. macOS/Linux recruits get the address and public CA from the backend team and
follow [Trusting the server](../learn/07-trusting-the-server.md).

Register on `https://<server-LAN-ip>/docs/` and wait for approval. One human has one account. Backend members and testers
register too and are approved **not ranked**. The backend's server health-check key is never distributed.

## 2. The setup script (recommended)

On **My progress** or **Connect your implementation**, select your implementation. The first approval creates an empty
**My frontend** candidate; edit its name/repository or add Alpha, Beta and Gamma. Each candidate owns its platform,
claims, proposals, evidence and connection key. Agent names are descriptive: several agents can work on the same app.
Each candidate is meant to be a complete terminal app on its own, with every workspace and screen for every facility
profile (guide *Getting started*): give each agent (or group of agents) its own candidate and repository, compare the
results, and nominate the one you judge best.

Download the setup for the selected candidate. It contains that candidate's private key. Windows PowerShell:

```powershell
$d = (New-Object -ComObject Shell.Application).NameSpace('shell:Downloads').Self.Path; $s = Get-ChildItem "$d\haspataal-connect*.ps1" | Sort-Object LastWriteTime | Select-Object -Last 1; if ($s) { powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $s.FullName } else { "No haspataal-connect.ps1 in $d - download it from the portal first." }
```

macOS/Linux Terminal:

```bash
d=$(xdg-user-dir DOWNLOAD 2>/dev/null); [ -d "$d" ] && [ "$d" != "$HOME" ] || d="$HOME/Downloads"; f=$(ls -t "$d"/haspataal-connect*.sh 2>/dev/null | head -n 1); if [ -n "$f" ]; then bash "$f"; else echo "No haspataal-connect.sh in $d - download it from the portal first."; fi
```

The script asks for the **repository folder**: an existing one, or a new one it offers to create (quotes around a pasted
or dragged path are fine). Alternatively pass `-ProjectPath "D:\Projects\Alpha"` on Windows,
or `--project /path/to/alpha` on macOS/Linux. Confirm the implementation ID it displays. It proves the CA, developer
and implementation before configuring the project. It merges the local settings, keeps backups and unrelated settings,
and sets shared CA/proxy support without a machine-wide active implementation or MCP key variable.

| Agent | Project-local configuration |
|---|---|
| Claude Code | Your home `.claude.json`, under `projects[absolute repository path].mcpServers.haspataal` (local scope) |
| Codex | The repository's `.codex/config.toml`, loaded only after you trust the project |
| Antigravity | The repository's `.agents/mcp_config.json`, `mcpServers.haspataal` with `serverUrl` |

Codex names the scoped connection `haspataal_project` and disables the old `haspataal` connection in that project.
This prevents an old user-level bearer-token setting from being merged into the new connection. Other repositories
retain their own settings.

Codex/Antigravity local files hold the private key. Setup excludes them and their backups in `.gitignore` and refuses
already tracked files. Never force-add them or distribute a working copy containing private settings. Update older
agents if they do not support workspace configuration. Project trust remains your decision in the agent.

Restart/reload each agent, call `my_progress`, and verify **both username and implementation ID**. Repeat setup for each
separate repository: configuring Beta must leave Alpha working. Different folders do not isolate the shared DEV demo
database; coordinate demo records and destructive scenarios with other developers.

Repeat setup is supported. Rotation affects only this candidate: download a fresh script and rerun it in its folders.
The server is its certificate, not its address: a repository connected at one address of the server (the office LAN)
moves to another (a VPN name for working from home) when you rerun setup downloaded from the portal at the new address,
because the hospital CA is the same. A repository of another server, developer or implementation is refused.
`-Remove` / `--remove` removes this folder's Haspataal entries; shared CA trust and other folders remain.
`-KeepScript` / `--keep-script` retains the downloaded secret-bearing script; otherwise successful setup deletes it
and older copies for the same developer, server and implementation. `-NoSystemChanges` / `--no-system-changes` skips
certificate/user-environment setup. It still edits this repository's local settings.

## 3. Existing developers and work

Existing code and Git history are untouched. Reconnect each repository using its candidate's script, then refresh the
agent's backend context. Old personal connections retain shared documentation but have no implementation context.
They cannot submit proposals and must be upgraded for personalized progress or roadmaps.

Old registry records appear under **Existing work - attribution needed**. Create an active candidate, open a legacy
screen, select the items you retested, name the tested build and describe your review. Save the screen to transfer
those claims to the target candidate ID. Previous verification stays historical; it is not duplicated. Historical
calls without a candidate ID remain unattributed. Penalties and inspection history stay attached to the person.

## 4. Propose, review and inspect

Agents call `propose_progress` with the current rubric fingerprint, screen/item IDs, commit/build, evidence and a
unique request ID. Evidence should identify source files, test results, reproduction steps, handbook coverage and
limitations, in 10-12000 characters (the tool's input schema states every limit). Repeating identical input with the
same request ID is safe; corrections use a fresh ID. A refused proposal is an error result that says its code and why
(`VALIDATION_ERROR` with `details.field`, `RUBRIC_CHANGED`, `REQUEST_CONFLICT`, `INVALID_STATE`): correct it and send
again, and never report it as saved.

The human reviews the proposed build on **My progress**, accepts specific items, or returns the proposal with reasons.
The **Agent proposals & human reviews** inbox groups readable screen cards by workspace, with the tested build,
agent, evidence and checklist. Current pending items start selected. After testing, click **Approve all reported
progress** to approve the displayed selection together; the button itself is your human declaration, shown above it.
Untick a proposal or individual items to approve only part of the work. A workspace's My progress page limits the
inbox to that workspace. New proposals arriving later are never included in your approval.

F1 help, role FAQs, zoom and the fresh-data review are accepted only with **your signed review** of the workspace on
the portal ([guide 17](17-workspace-review-checklist.md)): a proposal card that reports them shows the review that
passes them on its screen, preselected, and leaves an item it does not pass unselectable. Extra review notes are
optional. Each proposal keeps its own build, accepted items, reviewer and review. The whole batch saves together: if a
checklist or screen revision changed, reload and review again before retrying. Nothing in that batch is partly
approved. **Return for correction** sends a proposal back with your explanation.

A pending proposal earns zero points. `progress_proposals` returns the human's feedback and the signed reviews'
failures (`human_reviews`). Agents cannot accept their own claims, nor start, fill or sign a review. Manual reporting
remains available and requires a build reference and declaration; the four compulsory items need the signed review there
too. Concurrent changes or inspections require reloading before a manual report can overwrite it.

Nominate one active candidate for the leaderboard: the implementation you judge best, which you may change later.
Scores never sum candidates or combine their screens. Archiving
retains history and removes a nomination. Backend inspectors select the exact candidate/build and confirm or withdraw
accepted claims. Verification is a subset of completion points, never a second award. Penalties and escalation follow
the developer across candidates. Human review reliability shows confirmed versus inspected claims, with sample size.

## 5. DEV app evidence

Send both `X-Haspataal-Developer: <username>` and `X-Haspataal-Implementation: <numeric ID>` on your app's DEV requests.
These headers are untrusted attribution, never authentication or proof of completion. The secret MCP key must never
be embedded in the frontend app. Missing implementation IDs produce unattributed evidence and never fill a candidate's
checklist. Sandbox calls are attributed by their MCP connection key and still earn no points.

DEV builds also have a **Review code** setting: one field for the whole app, in **Settings → This terminal** (the tier
that also opens before login, since the tester logs in as several roles), empty by default. It is not on any screen nor
on the login form. When the human tester starts a review on the portal, they type its code there; while it is set, the
shared API client sends `X-Haspataal-Review: <code>` on every request, and the server counts those writes, and only
those, as the tester's review (the fresh-data review needs them). The coding agent builds the setting and never fills
it, in tests or scripts; its own writes appear apart in the review, without the code.

All three headers and the field sit behind the DEV build flag (`BuildConfig.DEBUG`, `#if DEBUG`, a `BUILD_IS_DEV`
constant): the release build a hospital installs is compiled without them (guide 19, I6 and I9).

## 6. Check it works and troubleshoot

| Symptom | Action |
|---|---|
| TCP timeout/unreachable | Run first-access diagnostics; ask IT to check the route/neighbor state, Wi-Fi/VLAN isolation, server address, listener and firewall |
| TLS/name/CA failure | Obtain a current handover bundle and verify its fingerprint; check certificate names and clocks |
| Wrong implementation in `my_progress` | Re-run the correct candidate's setup in the actual project root; reload and accept project trust |
| "Connected to another Haspataal server" | The folder belongs to a server with another CA, or this computer kept no copy of the old one's CA: run that server's setup with `-Remove` / `--remove`, or choose the right folder |
| Legacy personal connection | Download the selected implementation's new script |
| Refused key | Account suspended, candidate archived, or key rotated; reconnect using an active approved candidate |
| Tracked local config | Remove private machine settings from version control before setup; preserve shared configuration separately |
| Stale tools | Reconnect and call `what_changed`, then refresh the roadmap/screen bundles |

Official configuration references: [Codex MCP](https://developers.openai.com/codex/mcp),
[Claude Code MCP scopes](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp), [Antigravity MCP](https://antigravity.google/docs/mcp).

## 7. Tell the agent to use it

The latest setup automatically maintains a **required progress reporting** block in the repository's `AGENTS.md`
and `CLAUDE.md`, preserving your other instructions. These files contain no credentials. Codex and Antigravity read
`AGENTS.md`; Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md` (Antigravity's [rules reference](https://antigravity.google/docs/rules/)).
Restart the agent after setup. If this repository was connected earlier, download and run its latest setup **once**
to install the requirement. Re-running updates the managed block; removing the connection removes that block only.

You do **not** need to keep asking for progress reports. After each implemented or materially updated screen, and
before switching workspace or handing off, the agent must submit tested checklist items with `propose_progress`,
verify them with `progress_proposals`, and give you the proposal IDs. For a workspace, it reports each affected screen.
It must avoid duplicating unchanged pending or accepted work. Unfinished work stays explicit; missing human review is
a limitation, never an invented result. If the server is unavailable, the agent saves the payload and request ID
without credentials, tells you reporting is blocked, and retries next session.

This is a mandatory agent workflow, not proof that every coding agent will obey: the backend cannot see unreported
local code. The **My progress** badge and the header's **awaiting review** link count saved pending proposals across
all your active implementations. They refresh every 30 seconds while the portal is visible and when you return to
it. Click the alert to open the relevant implementation; review links load new proposals without an automatic refresh
discarding an unfinished review. Accepted or returned proposals leave the count; archived implementations are excluded.

The installed rules direct the agent to this full workflow. The reference block below can also be kept alongside
your own repository instructions:

```markdown
## The backend
The hospital backend (Haspataal) is the single source of truth: the UI holds no business rule. Before coding against it:
1. Call the Haspataal MCP connection's `overview` once per session (`haspataal_project` in Codex, `haspataal` elsewhere),
   then `get_build_roadmap()`: build in its order (the
   capabilities of Phase 0 first, then the screens ready next); `search` for anything else.
2. Per screen: `get_screen_bundle(screen_id)` has everything to build it (rules, endpoints with who may call them,
   fields, errors, what a lost answer means, realtime, states, test plan, handbook page, scenarios, examples).
   Follow `get_ui_quality_brief(screen_id=...)` before building and during review; use `workspace=...` for the whole
   role journey. Fetch omitted bundle sections. `get_workflow_recipe(slug)` gives a hospital workflow with real payloads.
3. Per endpoint: `get_endpoint(method, path)` for the contract and a recorded example; `generate_typescript` for typed calls;
   `validate_request` before writing a payload. Never hand-write a request shape.
4. Bring each state up with `sandbox_scenario(id)`, try calls with `sandbox_call` as the screen's demo account and
   `sandbox_events`; test with `screen_test_plan(id)`; after a backend update run `what_changed`. Submit evidence-backed
   drafts with `propose_progress` after EVERY implemented or materially updated screen, before switching workspace or
   final handoff, without waiting to be asked. Verify with `progress_proposals` and give the human the proposal IDs.
   Do not duplicate unchanged pending or accepted work; retain the payload/request_id and report a blocker if posting fails.
   Only the human's portal review awards progress. `my_progress` shows accepted claims
   and what is still open; `progress_proposals` shows review feedback.
5. Decide by permission (from /auth/me), never by role name; follow pdf_download for sets of documents (never a ZIP);
   the PHC inspection and web portal screens cite MSDS indicators: `get_msds_indicator` explains each.
6. Never invent a value only people can decide (a colour, a sound, how an event is shown, masks, digits):
   `open_decisions` lists them with what to do meanwhile.
7. Ship the end-user handbook with the screens: `get_end_user_handbook_brief`, `get_handbook_outline(workspace)`.
   Explain every control and outcome in English and Urdu; include a workspace guide and detailed role FAQs for every
   supported task. Maintain frontend coverage checks and obtain a named human journey/translation review. Passing
   API tests alone is insufficient; report missing evidence as pending. Submit evidence with propose_progress; never invent human approval or award progress.
8. F1 contextual Help and detailed FAQs for every supported workspace role are compulsory. Implement Ctrl/Cmd +, -,
   and 0 with one shared keyboard/Settings zoom state clamped to 100–250% (reset 100%). Before completion, a named
   human follows get_guide('workspace-review-checklist') and signs the review on the portal: fresh-data CRUD through
   the app, not just seeded records; supported cancellation/correction instead of forbidden deletion. Build the DEV
   Review code setting (X-Haspataal-Review; get_ui_quality_brief → dev_build_headers) and never set a code yourself.
   Missing help, FAQs, zoom or review means pending; fix the failures `progress_proposals` → `human_reviews` lists.
9. Start every session with `my_progress`: its `backend_issues` lists the backend team's answers to your reports since
   you last read them. Read them with `my_backend_issues`; re-test a Fixed one once `server_build` is at or after its
   `fixed_in`. Found the backend wrong or missing something? `report_backend_issue` (guide 20), never a frontend workaround.
```

## 8. Test your connection from home

Working from home through a VPN such as NetBird? **Connect your agent** has a **connection test** for Windows. Download
it there, open PowerShell (not as administrator) and paste:

```powershell
$d = (New-Object -ComObject Shell.Application).NameSpace('shell:Downloads').Self.Path; $s = Get-ChildItem "$d\haspataal-network-test*.ps1" | Sort-Object LastWriteTime | Select-Object -Last 1; if ($s) { powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $s.FullName } else { "No haspataal-network-test.ps1 in $d - download it from the portal first." }
```

It takes about a minute, changes nothing, and writes `haspataal-network-report-<you>-<date>.md` to your Downloads
folder. Send that file to the backend team. It checks, from your computer:

| Part | What it tells |
|---|---|
| NetBird | Connected or not; **direct (P2P)** or **relayed**; NetBird's latency; quantum resistance |
| The server | Its name resolves to NetBird addresses only; which of its addresses answer from here (an office address does not, at home) |
| Quality | Connection and request times: median, jitter, failed attempts; the transfer rate of small files (what the app and your agents see, not your line's full speed) |
| Security | The certificate pinned to the hospital CA; TLS version; HSTS; HTTP only redirects; the Control Center and the internal routes refused; the MCP server refusing a call without a key; live updates; terminal discovery; every other port of the server closed to you |
| This computer | Windows Firewall on; the NetBird adapter's network type |

The report starts with a summary: **PASS**, **ATTENTION** (something to look at) or **FAIL**, and a quality, security
and privacy level. A relayed link works but is slower; a FAIL names what to fix. The report holds no key, password or
patient data, and masks public internet addresses.
